documents.text: A neutron star is the collapsed core left behind when a massive star explodes as a supernova. A typical neutron star holds about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun in a sphere only about 20 kilometers across. That makes neutron star matter one of the densest forms of matter known.

documents.title: Neutron star matter density (offline fixture)
documents.publisher: AI Studio offline fixture, not a real publication
documents.text: A piece of neutron star matter the size of a sugar cube would weigh about a billion tons on Earth. The matter only stays this dense because of the star's enormous gravity; removed from the star, it would decompress violently. What exists in the innermost core is still unknown, and some models suggest exotic states such as free quarks.

editorialIntent: Let viewers guess the weight of a sugar cube, reveal the neutron star scale, then flip it with the thought experiment that the cube would burst apart outside the star.

segments.narration: Guess what this sugar cube weighs?
It is not sugar. It is a scrap of a neutron star, the collapsed core left behind when a massive star explodes as a supernova.
Now squeeze about 1.4 times the mass of our Sun into a ball only 20 kilometers across.
Packed that tightly, a piece the size of a sugar cube would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
But if you could carry it home, it would not stay small. Without the star's gravity holding it together, it would burst apart violently.
And deeper inside, nobody knows for sure what the matter becomes. Some models suggest it might even break down into free quarks.
A spoonful of star you can only weigh with math. What question would you ask it? Follow IFNOVA for more strange science.
